summary: Defines terms used in work on IP mobility. It came out of the Seamoby working group but was written to be useful for any IETF group dealing with mobility. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3753 gives engineers a shared vocabulary for talking about devices that move between network connections. It defines terms for access networks, handovers, paging, and mobility security. It introduces terminology, not a protocol.

subtitle: Shared definitions for discussing IP mobility and handovers.

tldr.problem: People working on IP mobility used terms differently, making technical discussions harder to follow across engineering groups.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3753 collects definitions for general networking, access networks, mobile nodes, handovers, paging, ad-hoc networks, and mobility security.
tldr.outcome: This Informational RFC is a vocabulary reference, not a protocol specification. It began in the Seamoby Working Group and is intended to be useful to other mobility-related work.

today: RFC 3753 is an Informational terminology document published in June 2004. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Mobility Terms Need Definitions
sections.content:
The document began in the Seamoby Working Group and aims to provide common terms for discussions about IP mobility. Its authors say the list is a first step toward harmonizing language among people with different engineering backgrounds, not an attempt to claim new terminology.

The general terms include routing and link concepts. The RFC also explains that terms such as Access Point and base station may describe the same component from an IP perspective, while Access Router describes a different role.
sections.plainLanguage: Different groups need consistent names for the parts involved when a device moves through a network. This document collects terms to support that shared discussion.

sections.title: Home and Care-of Addresses
sections.content:
A Home Address is the permanent IP address of a mobile node on its home link. A Care-of Address is associated with the node while it visits a foreign link.

A Home Agent is a router on the home link that intercepts packets for the Home Address and tunnels them to the registered Care-of Address. A Binding Update tells others about a node's current mobility binding, including its Care-of Address.
sections.plainLanguage: A mobile node keeps a Home Address while away from its home link. A Home Agent can forward packets for that address to the node's current Care-of Address.

sections.title: Access Networks and Mobile Nodes
sections.content:
An Access Network contains routers near the network edge that provide mobility support. An Access Router provides IP connectivity to mobile nodes and connects to one or more Access Points. An Access Network Gateway separates the access network from other IP networks; a gateway may also serve as an Access Router.

A Mobile Node can be a Mobile Host, which does not forward packets, or a Mobile Router, which does. A mobile network can move as a unit behind a Mobile Router, which has interfaces toward the mobile network and toward the wider network.
sections.plainLanguage: Access Points provide the link, while Access Routers provide IP connectivity near the network edge. A moving node can be a host or a router that carries an entire network with it.

sections.title: Handover Types and Goals
sections.content:
A handover is a change, or attempted change, in an active mobile node's point of attachment. It can stay within one Access Network or move to another. The document also distinguishes horizontal handovers between access points of the same type from vertical handovers between different types.

Handover can be classified along five mostly independent axes: who initiates it, who controls it, whether the mobile node or network assists, whether the previous or new router handles the move, and whether the move is planned. Make-before-break creates a new connection before ending the old one; break-before-make ends the old one first.

Performance terms describe different goals: smooth handover aims to reduce packet loss, fast handover aims to reduce latency, and seamless handover aims to avoid a noticeable change in service.
sections.plainLanguage: A handover moves a device's connection from one access point or network to another. The terms distinguish how the move is managed and whether the goal is fewer lost packets, less delay, or unchanged service.

sections.title: Paging, Mobility States, and Security Terms
sections.content:
A Mobile Node is in one of three states. In Active state, the network knows its Serving Access Router and the node can send and receive IP packets. In Dormant state, the network knows its Paging Area and must page the node before delivering packets. In Inactive state, the node is not listening for packets.

Paging moves a Dormant node to Active, while location updating tells the network that the node has entered a new Paging Area. Later sections define terms for context transfer, ad-hoc networks, and mobility security, including security associations and the Security Parameter Index.
sections.plainLanguage: The three states describe whether a device can exchange packets, is waiting to be paged, or is not listening. The glossary also defines terms for transferring network state and protecting mobility messages.
